Hacker News #8

万能钥匙不是陷阱

Passkeys are not a trap

科技产品 作者 speckx 热度 612 回复 752 2026/10/14 23:15
打开原帖 打开外部链接 JSON

摘要

  • A post called Passkeys are a trap. Do not use them. has been doing the rounds over the last few days, making it pretty high on Hacker News, and I've had it sent to me many times with an 'is this true?' kind of vibe. It's written for "non-technical citizens of the web", and the headline advice is to stop using passkeys and go back to TOTP codes and passwords.The ArgumentThe post makes what appears to be one central claim: Passkeys support something called attestation, which lets a website ask for cryptographic proof of what made the passkey.The author calls this a "hidden dial" and argues that sites will slowly turn it up, until you're only allowed to log in with approved software on an approved operating system, with no modifications, no LineageOS and no sharing your Netflix password. Throw in uBlock Origin, the FIDO Alliance membership list and the UK's image-scanning proposals, and the conclusion is that passkeys are "not designed to prioritize your interests". <that-escalated-quickly.gif>It's a compelling story. It just doesn't match how any of this actually works...Your Passkeys Don't AttestThe passkeys most people use are synced passkeys, stored in iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden or whatever other software of your choosing. These passkeys don't give websites an attestation statement at all, and though a site can ask, what comes back is none. I know this because I wrote an opensource passkeys library and made it available to everyone. If a consumer website decided tomorrow that it would only accept attested passkeys, it would lock out almost all of its own users, instantly. What website is going to do that? Besides, the guidance for consumer sites has been to not even request attestation for years now.Attestation Isn't What You Think It IsThe post describes attestation as proving "that an approved passkey manager, operating system, and firmware are in use" which is simply not true.When it is present, WebAuthn attestation tells the site the make and model of the authenticator, identified by its AAGUID, with a certificate chain from the vendor to back it up. It says nothing about your OS, your browser, your extensions, whether your phone is rooted or jailbroken, your firmware version, or even what colour it is.The YubiKey RecommendationThis is the part that surprised me the most. For people who want stronger security, the post recommends a hardware security key like a YubiKey, because it "avoids OS-wide attestation".YubiKeys are the authenticators that do attestation. Every one of them ships with a Yubico-issued attestation certificate, and enterprise attestation exists specifically so organisations can require approved hardware keys. I'd still recommend a YubiKey to anyone who wants one, they're excellent and I use them, but if attestation is the thing you're worried about, the post's own recommendation pushes you towards attestation rather than away from it!TOTP Is a Step BackwardsThe post holds up TOTP as "already" a great solution. TOTP is better than a password alone, absolutely, but it has one big weakness: you can type the code into the wrong website, just ask my good friend Troy Hunt. Phishing kits like Evilginx sit in the middle, relay your password and code to the real site in real time, and walk away with your session. This isn't theoretical, it's how a huge number of account takeovers happen today and we have the evidence to prove it. This is the problem that passkeys solve. A passkey is bound to the domain it was created for, so your browser simply won't use your example.com passkey on examp1e.com. There's no code to read out and nothing for the user to get wrong. The author even concedes this in the addendum, saying that passkeys are domain-bound and resist man-in-the-middle attacks, but still tells readers to avoid them. Swapping a phishing-resistant credential for a phishable one is a really bad trade...What You Should DoKeep using passkeys! Wherever a site offers one, take it, and store it in a password/passkey manager you trust. If you want to be able to move your credentials around, pick a provider that supports that. If you're worried about attestation creeping into consumer logins, then that's worth pushing back on, loudly (if it ever happens). But it hasn't happened, the biggest providers don't support it, and avoiding passkeys today while you wait for it won't protect you from anything, it just leaves you open to phishing.SourcesI have some experience in this area:I created WhyNoPasskeys.com to track the availability of passkeys on the Web. I built and deployed passkeys support on my own SaaS company.We built our own passkeys library and had it security reviewed.I wrote about Security considerations when using Passkeys on your website.I wrote Passkeys 101: An Introduction to Passkeys and How They Work.I made our passkeys library opensource for everyone to use.I've done extensive security testing of passkeys implementations. I've openly acknowledged the limitations of not using attestation on passkeys.I think most of all that it's important to say I use passkeys everywhere I can because they're currently the best thing we have available to protect our accounts. And they're not a trap. I don't know enough to argue about whether passkeys are a trap or not, but I do know as a user that they appear to be a confusing mess.

When a website prompts me to set up a passkey, depending on the device I happen to be using at the time it could end up going to Google password manager, Samsung password manager, iCloud Keychain, or Windows somethingorother.

What happens when I go to the same site on a different platform? What if I can't use cross-device authentication because I'm on a locked-down work machine or one that simply doesn't have bluetooth? What if I want to consolidate them all in one platform just for the sake of being organised? What if I lose or simply don't have the device with a certain passkey near me?

I don't have the time or patience to work out any of that, which might absolutely be a 'me' problem, but TOTPs are pretty sodding frictionless in comparison. Scan QR in my chosen manager; type number into website; done. Why are passkeys better?

vel0city 2026/10/15 07:30
几十年来我使用过许多密码管理器。由于糟糕/恶意的网站设计，需要对尚未配置插件的浏览器/应用程序进行身份验证，检测正确站点的插件存在错误等，我仍然不得不时不时地复制和粘贴密码。最后，如果用户可以将其复制并粘贴到任何地方，那么用户将将其复制并粘贴到任何地方。

同时还有其他安全优势。使用密码时，该静态凭证将在握手中传输。它可能会在两者之间的某个地方处理不当，现在整个根凭证可能会受到损害。这对于密钥来说是不可能的。凭证永远不会离开客户。在一些实现中，凭证永远不会离开安全飞地，甚至永远不会进入客户端的系统内存。对于密码，你不能说同样的话，甚至不是很接近。

I've used a number of password managers over decades. I'm still having to copy and paste passwords from time to time due to poor/hostile website designs, needing to authenticate into a browser/app that doesn't have the plugin configured yet, bugginess on the plugin detecting the right site, etc. And in the end, if the user can copy and paste that wherever, the user will copy and paste that wherever.

Meanwhile there are other security benefits as well. With a password, that static credential is transmitted in the handshake. It can be mishandled somewhere in between, and now that entire root credential is potentially compromised. This is just impossible with a passkey. The credential never leaves the client. In some implementations, the credential never leaves a secure enclave, never even entering the client's system memory. You can't say the same for passwords, not even close.
